title: Twenty First Word First Station Weariness In Prayer And Address To The Nafs

questions.question: What teaching from the Qur’an is mentioned near the beginning of the passage about the prayers?
questions.answer: It says that the prayers are required for believers at set times.

questions.question: What complaint did the older man make about praying?
questions.answer: He said praying five times every day felt too much and became tiring because it keeps repeating.

questions.question: When the speaker later listened to his own inner self, what did he notice?
questions.answer: He noticed that his own nafs was saying the same complaint.

questions.question: What reason is given for why the nafs spoke that way?
questions.answer: It was listening through laziness and taking that idea from Satan.

questions.question: What did the speaker understand about those words after hearing them again in himself?
questions.answer: He understood that they represented the voice of the evil-commanding soul and were influenced by whisperings.

questions.question: Why did the speaker decide to start with himself instead of others?
questions.answer: He realized that a person who has not corrected his own nafs cannot properly guide other people.

questions.question: How does the speaker describe the state in which the nafs said those words?
questions.answer: He describes it as ignorance mixed together, laziness, and heedlessness.

questions.question: What was the speaker planning to give his nafs in response?
questions.answer: He was going to give it five warnings.

questions.question: Who is being addressed directly in most of this passage?
questions.answer: The speaker’s own nafs, or lower self.

questions.question: What kind of person first spoke the complaint about prayer?
questions.answer: He was someone advanced in age, strong in body, and high in status.

questions.question: What positive thing did that man still say about the prayers before complaining?
questions.answer: He admitted that the prayers are good.

questions.question: What was his main problem with them?
questions.answer: He thought doing them every day five times was excessive and exhausting.

questions.question: How much time passed before the speaker reflected on that complaint in himself?
questions.answer: A long time passed.

questions.question: What does the phrase about the “ear of laziness” show about the nafs?
questions.answer: It shows that laziness makes the nafs ready to accept bad suggestions.

questions.question: According to the passage, what source was feeding the nafs this complaint?
questions.answer: Satan was feeding it that complaint.

questions.question: What does the speaker’s response teach about self-improvement?
questions.answer: It teaches that a person should first work on fixing his own inner faults before trying to fix others.

questions.question: What is the main issue being discussed in this passage?
questions.answer: The passage discusses why some people feel burdened by praying five times daily and how that objection should be answered.

questions.question: How is the older man’s objection described in simple terms?
questions.answer: He felt the prayers were good in themselves, but too frequent to keep doing every day.

questions.question: What happened when the speaker examined his own inner self?
questions.answer: He found the same objection inside himself.

questions.question: What does this discovery suggest about the problem?
questions.answer: It suggests that this is not just one person’s problem but a common struggle of the human nafs.

questions.question: What connection does the passage make between laziness and Satan?
questions.answer: It shows that laziness opens a person up to Satan’s whispering.

questions.question: Why does the speaker say he must begin with his own nafs?
questions.answer: Because personal reform has to come before guiding others.

questions.question: What kind of condition was the nafs in when it made those excuses?
questions.answer: It was in a state of idleness, heedlessness, and deep ignorance.

questions.question: What structure does the speaker announce at the end of the passage?
questions.answer: He announces that he will answer with five warnings.

questions.question: According to the passage, are the daily prayers presented as random or scheduled?
questions.answer: They are presented as scheduled acts of worship at appointed times.

questions.question: What feeling about repetition is expressed by the older man?
questions.answer: He feels that repeating the prayers every day makes them wearisome.

questions.question: Did the speaker reject the older man’s words right away as only that man’s problem?
questions.answer: No, because later he heard the same thing in his own nafs.

questions.question: What inner weakness allowed the nafs to receive that message?
questions.answer: Laziness allowed it to receive that message.

questions.question: What spiritual danger is pointed out by saying the idea came from Satan?
questions.answer: It warns that excuses against worship can come from harmful whisperings, not from sound thinking.

questions.question: What principle about leadership and advice is taught in the passage?
questions.answer: A person should correct himself first, because someone who cannot manage his own nafs is not ready to reform others.

questions.question: How does the speaker talk to his nafs after reaching that conclusion?
questions.answer: He speaks to it firmly and directly, calling it to listen.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the five warnings?
questions.answer: They are meant to answer the nafs’s complaint and wake it up from its careless attitude.

questions.question: What does the passage say believers are required to do regarding prayer times?
questions.answer: Believers are required to perform the prayers at specific appointed times.

questions.question: What two parts are found in the older man’s statement about prayer?
questions.answer: First he praises the prayers, and then he complains that praying five times daily is too much.

questions.question: Why does the complaint focus on the number of prayers rather than their value?
questions.answer: Because he says the prayers are good, but the repeated daily practice feels heavy to him.

questions.question: What did the speaker learn by listening carefully to his own nafs?
questions.answer: He learned that the same resistant attitude was living inside himself too.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the nafs as receiving bad ideas?
questions.answer: It describes the nafs as hearing through laziness and picking up a harmful lesson.

questions.question: What broader lesson did the speaker take from this about human souls?
questions.answer: He understood that such excuses speak in the name of the evil side of the self.

questions.question: Why is beginning with one’s own nafs an honest approach?
questions.answer: Because it means a person is not pretending to fix others while ignoring his own faults.

questions.question: What is the tone of the speaker’s final words to the nafs in this passage?
questions.answer: The tone is serious, corrective, and warning.

questions.question: What subject from the Qur’an frames this short section?
questions.answer: It frames the section with the teaching that prayer is required at appointed times for believers.

questions.question: How is the man who complained described before his words are given?
questions.answer: He is described as old, physically impressive, and socially important.

questions.question: What exactly made the man feel worn out about prayer?
questions.answer: He felt worn out because the five daily prayers continue every day without stopping.

questions.question: What surprising thing did the speaker discover after much time had passed?
questions.answer: He discovered that his own nafs was repeating the same complaint.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about the source of such complaints against worship?
questions.answer: It suggests they come from the evil-commanding self and from satanic prompting.

questions.question: What self-criticism does the speaker make before teaching anyone else?
questions.answer: He admits that if he has not reformed his own nafs, he cannot reform others.

questions.question: Which bad qualities are linked to the nafs’s words in the final sentence of the passage?
questions.answer: They are linked to mixed ignorance, laziness, and heedlessness.

questions.question: What does the speaker prepare his nafs for at the end of the passage?
questions.answer: He prepares it to hear five warnings that answer its excuse.
